LONDON, England (CNN) -- Thousands of documents about reported UFO sightings -- ranging from calm accounts by professional pilots to unhinged rants about the extraterrestrial menace -- have been released by the British Ministry of Defence. Taiwan resident Lee Chun-hung took these pictures showing a ball of fire trailing across the sky. The 4,500 pages cover sightings that were reported from 1986 through 1992. The British military released them to a curious public as part of a four-year project to transfer all such documents to the National Archives. One highlight from the batch released Monday involves the captain of an Italian airliner. He shouted "Look out!" to his co-pilot in April 1991 after claiming to see a beige "missile-shaped object" shoot past the cockpit. In that instance, the defence ministry ruled out a missile and "all the usual explanations," wrote David Clarke, a UFO expert and journalism instructor at Sheffield Hallam University, who worked with the National Archives to prepare the new materials for release. "The end result was this was a genuine UFO and the file was simply closed," he wrote. "There was nothing more they could do." The newly released documents also carry an account by a U.S. Air Force pilot who says he was told to shoot down an unidentified flying craft over eastern England. But before he could fire, the object disappeared. The next day, a man arrived to debrief the pilot and "he was told in no uncertain terms that what he had seen on his radar was top secret and he wasn't to speak about it to anyone," Clarke wrote. The first set of files was made available to members of the public in May. It covered reported UFO sightings from 1978 to 1987, and included hundreds of police reports taken from witnesses who described seeing lights or strange objects in the sky. People who reported having seen UFOs typically describe various shapes and colors of lights, moving in formation or hovering in the sky. Witnesses reported orange, red, white and green lights that were diamond-shaped, square, or cigar-shaped. They reported them to police, who have a standard 16-question form specifically for UFO sightings. "The vast majority of them are just ordinary people who've seen something unusual and thought that they ought to tell someone about it," Clarke has said. The Ministry of Defence said it examined the reports solely to determine whether enemy aircraft had infiltrated British airspace. Once it was determined that no enemy aircraft were in the sky, it did not investigate further. "The Ministry of Defence has no other interest or role regarding UFO matters and does not consider questions regarding the existence or otherwise of extraterrestrial life-forms," it said in May. That left many incidents unexplained.

For decades, public fascination with Unidentified Flying Objects (UFOs) was often dismissed as the realm of science fiction and conspiracy theories. However, a major historical release from the British government has revealed that behind closed doors, defense officials were taking these aerial anomalies very seriously. 

To satisfy decades of intense public curiosity and promote governmental transparency, the British Ministry of Defence (MoD) officially transferred a massive cache of 4,500 pages of documented UFO sightings to the National Archives in Kew. Covering the turbulent period from 1986 to 1992, this extensive release marks a key phase in an ongoing, four-year declassification project aimed at opening the nation's "X-Files" to researchers, historians, and the public alike.

The newly published documents—comprising handwritten eyewitness reports, official memo chains, radar logs, and defense transcripts—paint a captivating picture of Britain’s airspace during the late Cold War era. Far from being restricted to vague lights reported by casual stargazers, a significant portion of the archive details heart-pounding, high-stakes encounters reported by highly trained aviation professionals. 

Among the most compelling accounts are those submitted by commercial airline captains and Royal Air Force (RAF) jet pilots. The files detail multiple instances where experienced aviators encountered strange, highly maneuverable craft operating in controlled airspace. In one notable incident documented in the files, a commercial air crew descending toward a major UK airport reported an oval, metallic object buzzing their aircraft at an impossible speed—an event subsequently corroborated by unusual primary radar returns that defied conventional physics. Other reports from military pilots describe scramble missions where interceptor jets chased luminous objects that accelerated instantly, leaving the world’s most advanced fighter craft far behind.

Following these incidents, MoD intelligence staff subjected each report to rigorous scrutiny. Investigators routinely cross-referenced sightings against weather balloon launch schedules, satellite re-entries, natural atmospheric phenomena, and secret military aviation tests. Yet, in dozens of high-profile cases, every standard explanation fell short. 

Rather than inventing forced explanations, defense officials were forced to draw a startling conclusion: the objects were real, their origins were unknown, and they posed a potential—if undefined—air safety hazard. Officially, these cases were filed away not as hoaxes, but as "genuine mysteries."

The release of these 4,500 pages does more than just indulge public fascination with the unknown; it highlights the serious, methodical, and often frustrated efforts of a national government attempting to monitor and safeguard its skies against the inexplicable. While the documents stop short of confirming extraterrestrial origin, they definitively prove one thing: deep within the heart of the British defense establishment, the question of what is flying in our skies was treated not as a joke, but as a matter of genuine national interest.

**LONDON** — The British Ministry of Defence (MoD) has officially completed the transfer of a vast collection of previously classified UFO files to The National Archives at Kew, offering the public an unprecedented look into decades of reported sightings, military investigations, and government secrecy.

Spanning more than 50 years—from the height of the Cold War through the late 2000s—the newly available records comprise tens of thousands of pages. The collection includes military radar logs, photographs, hand-drawn sketches, and witness accounts from commercial pilots, military officers, and members of the public.

Among the declassified materials are detailed files on Britain’s most famous unexplained events, including the 1980 Rendlesham Forest incident, frequently referred to as "Britain’s Roswell." Documents show how U.S. Air Force personnel stationed at RAF Bentwaters reported mysterious glowing lights and a physical craft landing in the Suffolk countryside over a series of nights. 

Other files document a wide variety of strange reports, ranging from triangular crafts hovering over major cities to lights trailing commercial airliners, and even a report of an unidentified object flying near the Houses of Parliament.

"These files reveal the extraordinary reality of working on the government's 'UFO desk,'" said Nick Pope, who led the MoD’s UFO investigation unit from 1991 to 1994. "While the vast majority of sightings turned out to be weather balloons, bright planets, or civilian aircraft, a small percentage remained genuinely unexplained. For decades, the government took these reports very seriously from a airspace security perspective."

Despite the intense public interest and conspiracy theories surrounding the release, the documents reinforce the MoD’s long-standing official conclusion: in over 60 years of logging reports, investigators found no evidence to suggest that any unidentified aerial phenomenon posed a military threat to the United Kingdom, nor was there any proof of extraterrestrial visitation.

It was this very conclusion that led the MoD to permanently shut down its UFO desk and hotline in 2009. Officials determined at the time that investigating such reports consumed valuable defense resources without offering any military or operational benefit.

The release of the files follows years of campaign efforts and Freedom of Information (FOI) requests by researchers, journalists, and ufologists seeking greater government transparency.

The files are now available for public viewing online through The National Archives’ website and in person at the reading rooms in Kew, West London. Historians and enthusiasts alike expect it will take years to fully analyze the massive treasure trove of documents, which represents one of the most comprehensive official archives of UFO data in the world.

The documents, released by The National Archives and spanning the years 1986 to 1992, offer a unprecedented look into the Ministry of Defence's (MoD) once-secret "UFO desk." 

Among the thousands of reports from credible military personnel, commercial pilots, and ordinary citizens, two dramatic incidents stand out—highlighting moments when unidentified aerial phenomena triggered high-level military responses.

### 'Shoot Him Down'

In one of the most chilling accounts featured in the newly released archive, a U.S. Air Force pilot based in England was ordered to open fire on a massive unidentified flying object hovering over the British countryside. 

According to the declassified files, Pilot Milton Torres was scrambled in his F-86D Sabre jet from RAF Manston in 1957—an incident painstakingly reviewed and documented by defence officials during the 1980s. Torres reported locking his radar onto an object the size of an aircraft carrier. 

Before he could pull the trigger, the object accelerated at an astonishing speed—estimated at over 7,600 mph—and vanished from radar screens. Torres was subsequently told by military officials never to speak of the incident, a silence he kept for decades until the files were reviewed.

### Near-Miss over Kent

The files also detail a terrifying near-miss involving a commercial airliner in April 1991. 

Achille Zaghetti, an experienced Italian pilot flying an Alitalia MD-80 from Milan to London’s Heathrow Airport, reported seeing a brown, cigar-shaped object dart directly over his aircraft while cruising at 22,000 feet over Kent. 

"Look out! Look out!" Zaghetti shouted to his co-pilot, according to the official transcript. 

The object, estimated to be about three meters long, crossed their path at high speed. British military radar later confirmed a brief, unidentified target in the area at the time of the sighting, but the MoD ultimately closed the investigation when no missile launch was detected and no origin could be traced.

### Behind the Secret Desk

While the public often associates UFOs with extraterrestrial life, the documents reveal that the British Ministry of Defence was primarily focused on national security and airspace integrity—particularly during the waning years of the Cold War.

"These files allow us to look behind the scenes of what was one of the MoD's most secretive desks," Dr. David Clarke, a UFO expert and journalism lecturer at Sheffield Hallam University who worked with The National Archives on the release, told CNN.

"Even if these documents don't provide definitive proof of alien visitations, they show just how seriously military officials had to take unexplained radar returns and pilot reports," Clarke said. "When a commercial pilot or a fighter jet captain reports a near-miss, it becomes a crucial matter of aviation safety and air defence, regardless of what the object actually turns out to be."

Clarke noted that the vast majority of sightings could be explained as weather balloons, bright planets, space debris, or unconventional military aircraft. However, a small percentage—roughly 5%—remained stubbornly unexplained.

The release is part of an ongoing project by the UK government to declassify its entire archive of UFO reports, a process that began in 2008. The Ministry of Defence officially closed its UFO investigation unit in 2009, concluding that in more than 50 years of monitoring, no report had ever suggested evidence of a potential military threat or extraterrestrial presence. 

Yet for historians, aviation experts, and enthusiasts combing through the 4,500 new pages, the files provide a fascinating glimpse into a time when the skies over Britain were watched with intense, official paranoia.

**LONDON** — Declassified documents released by the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) have unveiled a vast archive of UFO sightings spanning over half a century, detailing everything from mid-air encounters by military pilots to bizarre civilian reports of alien abductions. 

However, despite decades of investigation, the British government’s official stance remains resolute: there is no evidence that extraterrestrial life has ever visited Earth, nor that Unidentified Flying Objects pose a threat to national security.

The documents—comprising tens of thousands of pages released in batches through The National Archives—cover reports logged by the MoD’s dedicated "UFO desk" from the 1950s until its closure in 2009. 

### Jet Chases, Bright Lights, and Pop Culture Spikes

The released files reveal a wide array of incidents reported by radar operators, police officers, commercial airline captains, and members of the public. 

Among the high-profile accounts included in the files is the 1980 Rendlesham Forest incident—often dubbed "Britain’s Roswell"—where U.S. Air Force personnel stationed in Suffolk reported seeing strange craft and glowing lights over several nights. Another prominent case, the 1993 "Cosford Incident," detailed reports from military personnel and police who witnessed a fast-moving, triangular craft flying over RAF bases in the Midlands.

The archives also highlight how public reporting often mirrored popular culture. The MoD noted a massive surge in UFO reports in 1996, coinciding with the peak popularity of the television show *The X-Files* and the release of the blockbuster film *Independence Day*. 

While many reports were attributed to misidentified aircraft lights, weather balloons, bright planets, or satellite debris, a small percentage of sightings remained officially unexplained due to a lack of detailed data.

### The Official Stance: Air Defence, Not Alien Hunting

Throughout the release of the documents, the Ministry of Defence reiterated its consistent policy regarding UFOs (officially termed Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, or UAPs). 

The government’s position states that the MoD’s sole interest in unidentified craft was to determine whether British military airspace had been breached by foreign hostiles or presented a threat to aviation safety. 

"The MoD exists to defend the UK," a defence ministry spokesperson stated regarding the file releases. "Over more than 50 years, no UFO report disclosed anything to suggest the presence of a military threat to the UK, nor was there any evidence to support the existence of extraterrestrial life."

The ministry consistently emphasized that it did not possess the mandate, expertise, or resources to act as an astronomical research body or to investigate claims of alien contact.

### The Closure of the UFO Desk

In December 2009, the MoD permanently closed its UFO hotline and dedicated investigation unit. Government officials concluded that maintaining the desk served "no defence purpose" and was diverting resources away from higher-priority military operations, particularly the ongoing war in Afghanistan.

Prior to its closure, the UFO desk was receiving hundreds of reports a year, the vast majority of which were deemed mundane or unsubstantiated. Officials noted that in more than 50 years of logging sightings, no report had ever alerted the military to a genuine national security threat.

Today, the complete collection of MoD UFO files is available to the public via The National Archives in Kew. While the government has closed the book on official investigations, the released documents continue to serve as a fascinating historical record of public fascination, atmospheric anomalies, and Cold War air-defence history.
